nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify Oxidizing and Reducing Agents
nodes.outcome: Identify the oxidizing agent and the reducing agent in a given chemical reaction

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Corrosion
nodes.outcome: Define corrosion as the slow deterioration of a metal when it is attacked by substances around it such as moisture and acids

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Describe Rusting of Iron
nodes.outcome: Describe the formation of a reddish-brown powdery coating on iron when exposed to moist air for a long time as rusting

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify Corrosion in Silver and Copper
nodes.outcome: Identify the black coating on silver articles and the green coating on copper objects as examples of corrosion

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Corrosion as Oxidation
nodes.outcome: Explain corrosion as an everyday oxidation process where metal atoms lose electrons and react with environmental agents

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Rancidity
nodes.outcome: Define rancidity as the condition produced by the oxidation of fats and oils in food, characterized by unpleasant smell and taste

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain the Cause of Rancidity
nodes.outcome: Explain that rancidity is caused by the oxidation of unsaturated fats and oils upon prolonged exposure to air and moisture

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Role of Antioxidants and Airtight Storage
nodes.outcome: Explain how adding antioxidants and storing food in airtight containers prevents or slows down the oxidation of fats

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Nitrogen Gas Flushing in Food Packaging
nodes.outcome: Explain why potato chip bags are flushed with unreactive nitrogen gas to prevent rancidity by creating an oxygen-free environment

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Heterotrophic Nutrition
nodes.outcome: State that heterotrophic nutrition is the mode where organisms depend directly or indirectly on autotrophs for carbon and energy

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Saprophytic Nutrition
nodes.outcome: Describe saprophytic nutrition as breaking down food materials outside the body and absorbing the nutrients, giving fungi like bread mould or yeast as examples

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Parasitic Nutrition
nodes.outcome: Describe parasitic nutrition as deriving nutrition from plants or animals without killing them, giving examples such as Cuscuta, ticks, lice, or tapeworms

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Holozoic Nutrition
nodes.outcome: Define holozoic nutrition as the intake of complex solid or liquid organic material that is subsequently digested and absorbed inside the body

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Describe Ingestion in Amoeba
nodes.outcome: Describe how Amoeba extends temporary finger-like extensions called pseudopodia to fuse over food particles and form a food vacuole

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Trace Digestion in Amoeba
nodes.outcome: Trace the breakdown of complex substances into simpler ones inside the food vacuole and their subsequent diffusion into the cytoplasm

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Egestion in Amoeba
nodes.outcome: State that remaining undigested material in Amoeba is moved to the surface of the cell and thrown out

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Describe Nutrition in Paramoecium
nodes.outcome: Explain how Paramoecium takes in food at a specific spot using the movement of cilia covering the entire cell surface

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Xylem Conducting Elements
nodes.outcome: Identify vessels and tracheids in xylem tissue of roots, stems, and leaves as forming a continuous water-conducting channel

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Root Pressure Mechanism
nodes.outcome: Explain that active ion uptake by root cells creates an osmotic gradient that moves water into root xylem, generating root pressure

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Transpiration Definition
nodes.outcome: Define transpiration as the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, primarily through stomata

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Transpirational Pull Mechanism
nodes.outcome: Explain how transpiration creates a suction pull that draws water and dissolved minerals upward through xylem to the leaves during daytime

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Translocation Definition
nodes.outcome: Define translocation as the transport of soluble products of photosynthesis, amino acids, and other substances through phloem tissue

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Phloem Sieve Tubes and Direction
nodes.outcome: State that phloem moves substances in both upward and downward directions using sieve tubes and companion cells

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Energy-Driven Translocation Mechanism
nodes.outcome: Explain that sucrose is loaded into phloem using ATP energy, causing water to enter by osmosis and creating pressure that moves material to tissues with lower pressure

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare Xylem and Phloem Transport
nodes.outcome: Compare xylem and phloem transport in terms of materials carried, direction of flow, and requirement of metabolic energy (ATP)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Gaseous Waste Excretion in Plants
nodes.outcome: Identify oxygen produced during photosynthesis and carbon dioxide produced during respiration as gaseous wastes eliminated through stomata and lenticels

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Elimination of Excess Water
nodes.outcome: Explain that plants eliminate excess water through transpiration via stomata

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Waste Storage in Vacuoles and Falling Leaves
nodes.outcome: Describe how plants store metabolic waste products in cellular vacuoles and eliminate them when aging leaves or parts fall off

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Excretion via Resins, Gums, and Roots
nodes.outcome: State that plants store waste products as resins and gums in old xylem and can also excrete some waste substances directly into the surrounding soil

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Properties of Convex Lens Real Images
nodes.outcome: Describe the position, nature, and relative size of real, inverted images formed by a convex lens when an object is placed at infinity, beyond 2F1, at 2F1, and between F1 and 2F1

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Convex Lens Virtual Image Formation
nodes.outcome: Explain why placing an object between the focus F1 and optical center O of a convex lens produces an erect, magnified, and virtual image on the same side as the object

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Concave Lens Image Characteristics
nodes.outcome: Describe the nature, size, and position of images formed by a concave lens when the object is at infinity versus at a finite distance from the lens

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Optical Instruments Using Lenses
nodes.outcome: Identify optical instruments such as magnifying glasses, cameras, microscopes, telescopes, and spectacles that use convex or concave lenses based on their image formation properties
